en: The Inquiry of Rāṣṭrapāla. Homage to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Noble Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas!
The First Chapter: The Introduction.
Thus have I heard.
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain, together with a great community of monks consisting of twelve hundred and fifty monks and five thousand bodhisattvas.

All of them possessed unimpeded eloquence, had attained patient endurance (*kṣānti*), had vanquished the adversaries that are the Māras, and had drawn near to all the qualities of a Buddha. They were bound by only one more birth, had attained the *dhāraṇīs*, had attained meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), and had attained infinite eloquence. They had reached the supreme perfection of unimpeded fearlessness, mastery over supernatural powers (*ṛddhivaiśāradya*), and so forth, until they had exhausted the description of all their virtues. Namely, there was the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named Samantabhadra; and...
and with the bodhisattva mahāsattva Samantanetra,
and Samantāvalokita, and Samantaraśmi, and Samantaprabha, and Uttaramati, and Vardhamānamati, and Anantamati, and Vipulamati, and Akṣayamati, and Dharaṇīdhara, and Jagatīṃdhara.
And with the bodhisattva mahāsattvas Jayamati, Viśeṣamati, and Dhāraṇīśvararāja;
with the sixty bodhisattvas headed by Mañjuśrī who possessed incomparable minds; with the sixteen virtuous men (satpuruṣa) led by Bhadrapāla;
and with Brahmā Sahāmpati, Śakra the lord of the gods, and the four world-protectors, including Susīma.

And there were the divine son Susthitamati and all the lords of the gods, lords of the nāgas, lords of the kinnaras, lords of the gandharvas, lords of the yakṣas, lords of the asuras, and lords of the garuḍas,
together with their retinues of many hundreds of thousands of various kinds, who had all assembled and taken their seats right there in that assembly.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One, seated upon the lion throne of glorious essence, rose up like Mount Meru above the entire circle of the assembly;
he illuminated the whole world like the sun and illuminated all living beings like the moon.
Like Brahmā, he dwells in perfect tranquility;
like Śakra, his body is difficult to assail;
like a universal monarch, he is endowed with the seven jewels of the factors of enlightenment.
Like a lion, he proclaims that all phenomena are devoid of self; like a mass of fire, he illuminates the entire world;
and like a sovereign jewel from the collection of all the radiant jewels of the gods, he blazes with splendor.

Having pervaded the entire trichiliocosm with his radiance, he— whose meaning was swiftly and definitively determined, who had attained the supreme perfection of all dharmas, and who was seated within the assembly— taught the Dharma with a voice like the sound of Brahmā’s speech, which follows after the communication of all sentient beings; a Dharma that is virtuous in the beginning, virtuous in the middle, and virtuous in the end.
He proclaimed the holy life (brahmacarya), which is meaningful in itself, well-expressed in its phrasing, exclusive, complete, pure, and purified.
Then, indeed, a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Prāmodyarāja was present and seated among that very assembly.

Seeing the Blessed One upon his lion throne—shining with extreme brilliance, eclipsing the entire circle of the assembly with a radiance exceeding a thousand suns—he became thrilled and joyful, his heart inclined toward serene faith. Rising from his seat, he joined his palms in reverence and praised the Blessed One with these verses:

Having surpassed these hosts of gods, asuras, kinnaras, and nāgas, as well as the disciples and sons of the Buddha, the Conqueror, possessing the splendor of Mount Meru, shines like the Golden Mountain itself. // 1 //
Like Mount Meru, the abode of the hosts of immortals, shining even while situated in the midst of the ocean;
so he, situated in the midst of the ocean of compassion, emits hundreds of thousands of rays of light. // 2 //
Abiding in the divine abodes (brahmavihāra), he shone like Brahmā dwelling in the city of Brahmā;
dwelling in meditation, liberation, and concentration, that supreme being illumines the entire world. // 3 //

Shining like Śakra among the thirty-three gods, the King of Sages, possessed of vast splendor, stands amidst the deities; adorned with the primary marks and rich in the qualities of wisdom, he illuminates the entire world. // 4 //
Indeed, as a ruler of the four continents, he shines, illuminating this world; and by leading beings onto the noble path, he who possesses a mind of compassionate intent shines forth. (5)
This sun-like Buddha shines in this world, emitting light like a gem of fire; he blazes in the sky as if moving toward it, his radiance surpassing that of a thousand suns.
Like the stainless moon at midnight, he shines, pure throughout all worlds;
the face of the Jina, resembling the full moon, blazes forth, outshining all other radiance. // 7 //

Just as a fire upon a mountain peak shines forth at the quieting of the night for the sake of sentient beings, so too does the Great Seer, having utterly destroyed the darkness of delusion, shine with the radiance of wisdom. // 8 //
Just as a lion on earth, with a deep roar from mountain caves, terrifies the deer, so too does a king,
with a voice proclaiming emptiness and selflessness, cause the rival heretics to tremble.
Like the king of true jewels, blazing with radiant splendor, he shines, surpassing all gems;
the body of the Victor, resembling the color of gold, shines, surpassing the entire world. (10)
There is no one equal to you anywhere in the world, nor is there any being found who surpasses you;
in terms of merit, wisdom, vigor, skillful means, and all virtuous qualities, there is no one equal to you. (11)
For the Hero among Men has illumined the world; I have seen the Lord, that ocean of virtues.
With joy increased by the arising of reverence, I have fallen at the soles of the feet of the Jina. 12.
Having praised Rūpasāgarabuddhi, the mine of all virtues and the lamp of the world, whatever merit has been acquired here by me through this, may the entire world attain supreme enlightenment. (13)
Then the bodhisattva mahāsattva Prāmodyarāja, having praised the Blessed One with these verses,
with palms joined in reverence and eyes fixed without blinking, gazed upon the body of the Tathāgata; contemplating the very realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu),
he entered into that which is profound, difficult to fathom, difficult to see, difficult to realize, beyond reasoning, transcending logic, peaceful, and subtle.
Contemplating the inconceivable domain of the Buddhas,
reflecting upon the Tathāgata’s wisdom that extends to all phenomena, and beholding the Buddha-realm which is unequaled and equal to all.

Entering into the inconceivable domain and range of the Tathāgatas' skillful means, conceiving of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, as having entered into the nature of the principle of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu),
and perceiving that the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, indeed have the non-abiding sky as their sphere of activity;
Resolving that all phenomena have the nature of entering the limit of reality which is itself without limit, longing for the unobstructed liberation of the Buddhas,
and penetrating the fact that the body of the Blessed Buddhas is constant, auspicious, and eternal;
Entering into the Tathāgata’s body, which pervades the expansions of all Buddha-fields and faces toward all sentient beings,
and recollecting that there is no end to the qualities of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, even throughout millions of eons until the furthest limit,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Prāmodyarāja remained silent, contemplating the very realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

Now at that time, the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla had entered the rains retreat for the three months in Śrāvastī. When the three months had passed, having prepared his robes and finished his robes, he took up his bowl and outer robe and, together with the community of monks— including novices, beginners, and those who had recently gone forth— traveled by stages on a journey through the countryside until he reached Rājagṛha.
He approached the great city in the direction of Vulture Peak, the king of mountains.
Then the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla, with palms joined in reverence, praised the Blessed One with these verses:
We pay homage to the best of men, the illuminator; we pay homage to him whose mind is equal to the sky. // 14 //
Leaders proclaim your praises from all directions across the expansion of millions of fields;
hearing this, the sons of the Buddha come with joy to worship the Sage, an ocean of virtues. (15)
Having performed worship in a manner befitting the Sugatas and having heard the stainless Dharma from the Great Sage,
they depart for their own realms with joyful minds as you proclaim that garland of praises.
For inconceivable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, you have practiced the course of conduct for the sake of sentient beings;
yet, while seeking supreme and excellent enlightenment, not even a weary thought has arisen in your mind.

O Leader, you have practiced generosity and morality, and you are trained in patience, vigor, and meditation; having always reached the perfection of wisdom and skillful means, for that reason you revere the Great Guide. (18)

We pay homage to the one who has reached the further shore of incomparable wisdom, who is skilled in the supreme super-knowledges of the bases of psychic power, who is trained in the faculties, the powers, and the liberations, and who has attained mastery over the conduct of all sentient beings. 19.
O Blessed One, supreme among men, you understand the mental continuum of the world, its conduct, and how karma arises; you also know the gateway of the method by which one is liberated. (20)
Abandon passion, hatred, and that which arises from delusion, by which beings go to the three lower realms;
know the well-done and ill-done deeds by which they go to a happy rebirth in the world. (21)
Those who have passed away in the past for the benefit of the world, those who are currently honored by humans and gods,
and those who will appear in the future having reached the further shore of supreme virtues— you know all those Sugatas.

You understand in every way and in its entirety the purification of the field, the manifestation [of the Buddha], the assemblies of bodhisattvas and likewise the śrāvakas, as well as the lifespan of the great sages. (23)

Whatever the state of the Dharma is in its cessation, and whatever the manner of worshiping the relics of the Jinas, and whatever the upholders of the treasury of Dharma are like therein— you know all those supreme among men. (24)
The wisdom of the One Possessing the Ten Powers is indeed known; it proceeds unobstructed and constantly throughout the three times.
O Victors, whose minds are endowed with the principles of all phenomena, you are oceans of wisdom—homage be to you! 25.
There is no one equal to you, much less superior; your body is adorned with the primary marks as the sky is variegated by stars. We pay homage to the best of sages, the supreme among men. 26.
Your form, too, which is peerless and enchanting, puts to shame the entire world including the gods; even Brahmā, Śakra, and the Akaniṣṭha deities do not shine in your presence. (27)
You are stainless like the mountain of gold; with smooth, glossy hair rising to the right, you shine like King Meru with its crown protruding, born of vast merit. // 28 //
From the region between your eyebrows, O King, you emit millions of billions of light rays;
with your lotus-like, enchanting eye, you behold the world with a heart of compassion. (29)
O Vināyaka, your face shines like the full moon in a cloudless sky; the beholder is never satiated. We pay homage to you, the one with the beautiful countenance, the supreme among men. (30)

With the stride of a swan, a peacock, and the king of beasts, and walking with the slow gait of an elephant in rut, you traverse the surface of the earth making it tremble; we pay homage to the One of Ten Powers, firm in his vows. 31.
The fingers of his hands are long, rounded, and beautiful; they are adorned with a web of nails that are pure copper-colored.
Standing upright, he can touch his kneecaps; we pay homage to him who resembles the color of gold.
You traverse the surface of the earth, adorning it with the strides of your feet marked by the patterns of wheels;
men who have been ripened by the rays of your feet, when they pass away, go to the world of the gods.
O King of Dharma, bestower of the seven kinds of wealth, lord of the gift of Dharma, with a tamed mind;
governing the world through the practice of Dharma, I bow to the Lord of Dharma, the Guide. (34)

With loving-kindness as armor, the supreme sword of mindfulness, and the bow of ethical discipline with the arrows of wisdom and skillful means—by these, the enemies that are the afflictions, which increase the craving for existence, birth, and death, have been destroyed. (35)
Having crossed over yourself, you ferry across millions of beings; being liberated, you release the world from its bonds.
You show the path that is secure and free from fever—the path by which the Sugatas go to the auspicious state. (36)
Where birth and death do not exist, nor separation, nor the arising of suffering—to that auspicious, supreme, unconditioned state you have indeed taught us, having taken recourse in compassion. (37)

Having praised the Great Sage, the Conqueror, the most excellent in the world, who has attained mastery over all phenomena—by whatever merit I have acquired herein, may the world awaken to enlightenment. (38)

Then the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla, having praised the Blessed One with these verses, rose from his seat with palms joined in reverence; he arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with joined palms toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "I would ask the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, about a certain matter."
“If the Blessed One would grant me the opportunity to ask a question and receive an answer,” [Rāṣṭrapāla said].
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla: “Ask, Rāṣṭrapāla, whatever you desire.
I shall satisfy your mind by answering each question that is asked.”

When this had been said, the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, endowed with which qualities does a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain the excellence of the qualities of the nature of beings, acquire knowledge that is not dependent on others, and attain swift wisdom?"
He attains the eloquence of definitive discernment and attains illumination;
he attains entry into omniscience, the ripening of sentient beings, the abandonment of perplexity, the abandonment of doubt, and the definitive certainty of omniscience.
What is skill in leading sentient beings into the path, acting in accordance with what one has spoken, speaking with intentional truth, and skill in dealing with sentient beings;
what is the attainment of the recollection of the Buddha and the ability to answer all questions;
and what is the retention of all dharmas—by means of these, how does one swiftly attain omniscience?
Then, at that time, the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla spoke these verses:
"The conduct of a bodhisattva is well-determined in its true nature; may the Jina, the supreme among men, speak for me the definitive discourse on the ocean of gnosis regarding its origin. (39)

O Supreme Being, best among men, whose body resembles refined gold and who has accumulated a mass of merit—you are indeed the protection, the refuge, and the final resort; tell me today of that stainless, supreme conduct. (40)
How does the lamp of knowledge come to an end? How is the dhāraṇī of the nectar of awakening attained?
How is the ocean of wisdom purified, so that one may cut through the doubts of people? (41)
Wandering through many millions of eons, he never once gives rise to a sense of weariness;
even upon seeing the world oppressed by suffering, he devotes himself to what is beneficial for them.

Reveal the perfection of the field and its retinue, the supreme lifespan, and the excellence of the realm; proclaim the unsurpassed discourse on the welfare of sentient beings and the stainless conduct of awakening.
O crusher of Māra, purifier of wrong views, dryer of craving, toucher of liberation! O jewel among beings, do not let the eye of the Dharma be obscured; practice this supreme conduct. (44)
With the perfection of physical form, enjoyments, and eloquence, and with gentle speech that delights the assembly,
you, O Sugata, like a rain cloud, satisfy the world and teach the domain of the Buddhas.
O Mañjughoṣa, with a voice as melodious as the kalaviṅka bird, possessing the Brahma-voice that destroys evil thoughts;
O Lord, you who desire the Dharma, satisfy this assembled assembly with the essence of the nectar of immortality. 46.
There is a desire for the most excellent and supreme enlightenment, yet the desire for the Dharma has not been established;
this is the time for the Teacher’s instruction, this is the time to hear the precious jewel.
O Sage, I have a longing for enlightenment; O Victor, you fully know my intention.
I do not seek to cause harm to the Victor; please, excellently, reveal the supreme conduct.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla: “Excellent, excellent, Rāṣṭrapāla!
It is well indeed, Rāṣṭrapāla, that you consider it necessary to question the Tathāgata regarding this matter.”
Rāṣṭrapāla, you have set out for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, and for the benefit and welfare of both gods and humans;
and you do so for the sake of supporting the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, of the present and the future.
Therefore, Rāṣṭrapāla, listen.
"Pay close and careful attention;
I shall speak.
"So be it, Blessed One," the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this to him: "Rāṣṭrapāla, a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with four qualities attains this purity.
What are the four?

That is to say: through practice with a resolute intention of pleasing [the Buddhas], through equanimity of mind toward all sentient beings, through the cultivation of emptiness, and through acting exactly as one speaks.
Endowed with these four qualities, Rāṣṭrapāla, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains this purity;
this is the nature of things here.
In this regard, it is said:
For those who are always devoted with noble intention to the path of awakening, their minds are irreversible;
in those possessors of infinite wisdom, there exists neither deceit, nor stubbornness, nor guile. (49)
Seeing beings suffering, leaderless, and oppressed by birth, sickness, old age, and death, they assemble the ship of Dharma for the sake of crossing over this world. (50)
Possessing a mind of equanimity toward all beings and being gentle, they regard the world as if it were an only son;
"I shall liberate all of this," such is the intention of those supreme persons. (51)
Having constantly attained mastery over the various forms of emptiness, one finds neither self nor sentient being;
for conditioned phenomena are like dreams and illusions, yet herein the ignorant and unawakened are utterly deluded. (52)
Just as those wise ones speak with their speech, so too do they abide in practice;
self-controlled, peaceful, always free from faults, and devoted to the path of the bodhisattvas—these are the sons of the Conquerors. (53)
Rāṣṭrapāla, there are these four qualities that provide bodhisattvas with consolation.
What are the four? They are:
the attainment of dhāraṇī, the attainment of spiritual friends, the attainment of receptivity toward the profound Dharma, and the practice of completely pure ethical discipline.
Rāṣṭrapāla, these four are the qualities by which bodhisattvas obtain consolation;
this is the natural law in this regard.
In this regard, it is said:
Those of great renown always become possessors of the *dhāraṇīs*,
by which they uphold the supreme Dharma spoken by all the Buddhas.
They never cause it to perish; rather, their delight increases further.
Their knowledge, which has reached the further shore of all phenomena, remains entirely unattached to them.
They obtain virtuous friends who increase the factors of enlightenment and teach them the supreme path by which the Leaders proceed;
they never become servants of evil friends.
They avoid from afar those who are burning by nature, as one would avoid fire.
Having heard the profound Dharma associated with emptiness, the steadfast ones do not, in any respect, hold views of a self, a sentient being, or a living soul.
They shall possess flawless ethical discipline, with minds that are peaceful and self-controlled;
you should establish them in that unsurpassed discipline of a Buddha.
Rāṣṭrapāla, there are these four qualities that bring joy to bodhisattvas who have entered into saṃsāra.
What are the four?
Rāṣṭrapāla, beholding the Buddha is a quality that brings joy to bodhisattvas.
Rāṣṭrapāla, hearing the Dharma that is in accordance with the truth is a dharma that brings joy to bodhisattvas;
so too is the relinquishing of all possessions and the patient acceptance of the non-apprehensibility of phenomena.
Rāṣṭrapāla, these are the four things that bring joy to bodhisattvas who have entered into saṃsāra;
this is the natural law in this regard.
In this regard, it is said:
They behold that Supreme among Men, the Perfectly Awakened One, illuminating all worlds with his splendor in every direction throughout all births.
Thus honoring him, O King of Men, established in love and reverence, they sought the supreme, foremost enlightenment for the sake of the liberation of all beings. // 57 //
He hears the peaceful and conformable Dharma from the Leaders;
having heard it with a resolute intention, the steadfast one applies himself through proper reflection.
Having heard the Dharma of non-apprehension, no doubt arises within him.
"Being devoid of a sentient being" means that the quality of a sentient being does not exist here; no self is found. (58)
He should become one who renounces all his possessions; thus, with a joyful mind and free from grasping, he should look upon the beggar who has approached him,
[offering] his village, kingdom, earth, children, wife, and even his own life.
They renounce everything, and no mental agitation arises in them. 59.
Rāṣṭrapāla, a bodhisattva should be free from attachment regarding four things.
Which four?
Rāṣṭrapāla, a bodhisattva should be free from attachment to living as a householder.
Having gone forth, Rāṣṭrapāla, a bodhisattva should be indifferent toward gain and honor;
Rāṣṭrapāla, a bodhisattva should be indifferent toward intimacy with families;
Rāṣṭrapāla, a bodhisattva should be indifferent toward body and life.
Rāṣṭrapāla, a bodhisattva should be free from attachment regarding these four qualities;
this is the natural law in this regard.

In this regard, it is said: Having abandoned the home, which is a thicket of endless faults, those virtuous ones— whose senses are stilled and who are gentle— always find delight in the forest, free from anxiety and worldly concern.
They have no intimacy with women, nor indeed with men anywhere;
they dwell alone, like rhinoceroses, pure in intention, stainless, and immaculate.
Their minds are not gladdened by gains, nor do they sink in the face of losses; having few desires, they find delight in one another, free from deceit and hypocrisy.
For the sake of sentient beings, with minds endowed with vigor, they are established in generosity and self-restraint;
having reached the further shore in meditation and the quality of vigor, they seek the wisdom of a perfectly awakened one.
Disregarding even their own bodies and likewise abandoning beloved kin,
those who are steadfast on the path to awakening and possess an adamantine resolve always apply themselves;
even if their bodies are cut into pieces, there shall be no wavering in their minds.
Desiring omniscience, they further exert very firm vigor in this world. // 62 //
Rāṣṭrapāla, there are these four qualities that cause Bodhisattvas to have no regret.
What are the four?
Rāṣṭrapāla, the non-breach of moral discipline is a quality that causes Bodhisattvas to have no regret.
Dwelling in the forest, avoiding contemptible people,
and following the four noble lineages—
Rāṣṭrapāla, the attainment of great learning is the quality that causes Bodhisattvas to have no regret.
Rāṣṭrapāla, these are the four qualities that cause Bodhisattvas to have no regret;
this is the natural law in this regard.
In this regard, it is said:

They guard their stainless morality like a precious jewel, yet they harbor no notion of "I" regarding that morality, nor do they think of themselves as being well-restrained; rather, they always establish sentient beings in that very same morality.
[He sees] this one desiring the supreme morality of a Buddha. // 63 //
For they dwell in empty and auspicious forests; there arises in them neither the notion of a self nor the notion of a living being.
They regard the form of sentient beings as equal to grass, wood, or a wall; here there is no woman, no man, and nothing belonging to a self.
Delighting in the four noble lineages, free from deceit and hypocrisy, they apply themselves with resolute intention;
being thus heedful, they always exert effort in the qualities of learning, aspiring for the great majesty of the Sugata’s wisdom. (65)
Beholding this world in the prison of existence— leaderless, struck by birth, old age, death, and sorrow, and afflicted by disease—
they have brought forth the excellent ship of the auspicious Dharma and ferry across the flood of the ocean of existence the multitudes of beings.
For there is no protector, no refuge, nor any final resort for the world wandering in the conditioned realm;
it is solely for the purpose of liberating all sentient beings that my vow was made for supreme enlightenment. (67)
Rāṣṭrapāla, there are these four ways of the well-bred horse that a bodhisattva should follow.
What are the four?
The attainment of a favorable rebirth,
which occurs through meeting with the appearance of a Buddha;
and service to one's teacher.
And that delight in remote lodgings is due to practicing without worldly motives;
and that is due to being indifferent toward gain and honor.
The attainment of eloquence,
which is through being endowed with the patient acceptance of the profound Dharma—
these, Rāṣṭrapāla, are the four ways of the thoroughbred that should be followed.
This is the nature of things here.
Regarding this, it is said:

The wise dwell constantly in forest caves; they are always without desire for gain. They are always possessed of eloquence and have unattached intellects; they are skilled in the profound Dharma and free from conceptual proliferation. // 68 //
They are always devoted to serving their gurus, and they apply themselves exactly as those gurus instruct them;
they please many immeasurable Sugatas and perform vast worship for the sake of the wisdom of the Jinas. (69)

The destiny of those of great resolve is indeed supreme; having reached the pinnacle among both gods and humans, they always encourage sentient beings toward the path of perfect enlightenment and likewise yoke them to the ten wholesome actions. (70)

And having heard of the qualities of a Buddha, they become joyful, for they will soon be near to me; they shall awaken to the auspicious, stainless, supreme enlightenment and liberate millions of beings from infinite suffering. (71)
Rāṣṭrapāla, there are these four qualities that purify the bodhisattva practice of bodhisattvas.
What are the four?
The bodhisattva practice of one who is not devoid of unimpeded consciousness.

Dwelling in the forest while avoiding hypocrisy, flattery, and extortion; desiring no karmic reward for the renunciation of all one's possessions; longing for the Dharma day and night; and not seeking out the faults of those who preach the Dharma.
Rāṣṭrapāla, these are the four qualities that purify the conduct of bodhisattvas.
Then, indeed, O Blessed One, at that time he spoke these verses:

"One who desires unsurpassed awakening is without stubbornness, impurity, or a mind of anger, nor does he seek out the faults of anyone else. He is free from deceit, free from hypocrisy, and his mind is devoid of conceptual proliferation. (72)

The home is exceedingly treacherous, the root of sorrow, and the source of association with wicked people; disregarding it from afar, those desiring liberation renounce the world and wander in mountain thickets after having gone forth. (73)

Frequenting various forest retreats, he remains independent in the attainment of all-knowledge; indifferent toward both body and life, he dwells like a lion, fearless and having conquered his enemies. // 74 //
And being content with whatever comes by chance, like a bird that has abandoned its hoarding, he has no fixed abode in any world; he constantly seeks knowledge on the path to enlightenment. (75)
He dwells alone just like a rhinoceros, and he does not tremble like a lion;
he does not place his trust in anyone on earth like a frightened deer, nor does he exult in being honored. (76)

Having beheld this world fallen into a precipice, I shall exert myself for the sake of its liberation; if I am to become a protector of this world, I must practice wholesome deeds with vigilance. (77)

Possessing very sweet speech, desiring smiles, and with a mind free from turbidity, he always dwells amidst the pleasant and unpleasant without becoming attached, like the wind; he does so while aspiring to this conduct of the best of men. (78)
Resolving upon emptiness, he courses in the signless; all conditioned things are, for him, like an illusion.
Delighting in tranquility and self-mastery, his intellect is vast, and he is forever satisfied by the nectar of immortality. // 79 //
As you respond, so too on the path to awakening, he constantly purifies his noble intention;
seeking the attainment of dhāraṇīs, he endures suffering, longing for the virtues of the virtuous. (80)
Having observed this finality, the Bodhisattva who becomes desirous of it would be satisfied;
but he who, being unattached here to awakening, gives rise to hundreds of faults, is one of small intelligence. (81)
Rāṣṭrapāla, there are these four precipices for bodhisattvas.
What are the four?
Rāṣṭrapāla, lack of respect is a precipice for bodhisattvas.
"Rāṣṭrapāla, ingratitude and the practice of deceit are a downfall for bodhisattvas.
Rāṣṭrapāla, attachment to gain and honor is a downfall for bodhisattvas.
Rāṣṭrapāla, the pursuit of gain and honor through hypocrisy and flattery is a downfall for bodhisattvas."
Rāṣṭrapāla, these are the four precipices for bodhisattvas.

Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses: “They are always lacking in respect even toward their noble teachers, their mothers, and their fathers; they are ungrateful and deceitful, and those fools are always unrestrained in their conduct. (82)
Always intent on gain, they are devoted to deceit and fraud; they will say, "There is no one here equal to me in any respect regarding my moral conduct and virtues. (83)
They are hostile toward one another and constantly engaged in seeking each other's faults;
devoted to agriculture and trade, for them, the state of a śramaṇa is indeed very far away. 84.
Thus, in the future time, those monks who are unrestrained will be far removed from the virtues of moral discipline;
under the influence of quarreling, strife, and envy, they will cause my Dharma to decline. 85.
They will always remain very far from the path to enlightenment and very far from the wealth of the noble ones;
having abandoned the sublime path to liberation, they will wander through the five realms of existence.
Rāṣṭrapāla, there are these four factors that create obstacles to the awakening of bodhisattvas.
What are the four?
Lack of faith, Rāṣṭrapāla, is a factor that creates an obstacle to the awakening of bodhisattvas.
Laziness, Rāṣṭrapāla, is a quality that creates an obstacle to enlightenment for bodhisattvas. Arrogance, Rāṣṭrapāla, is a quality that creates an obstacle to enlightenment for bodhisattvas.
A mind of envy and stinginess toward the honor shown to others, Rāṣṭrapāla, is a quality that creates an obstacle to enlightenment for bodhisattvas.
Rāṣṭrapāla, these are the four qualities that create obstacles to the enlightenment of bodhisattvas.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:

"Those who lack faith, are indolent, always deluded in mind, conceited, and ever prone to anger—even they, seeing a patient monk who is constantly disciplined, will inflict punishment upon him as he departs from the monastery. (87)
Envy has arisen here for the sake of another's honor; yet there is no such state of mind toward them.
Seeking a point of entry and searching for a lapse, [one thinks]: "What fault is there here that I might urge against him? (88)
Far indeed from my teaching are those who hate its virtues, for they are inclined toward ruin;
having abandoned even the teaching of the Jina, they shall go to a blazing and fierce state of woe. (89)

Having heard here of their evil conduct and their most dreadful destiny joined with unrighteousness, you should always apply yourselves to the path to awakening; do not suffer when reborn in the miserable realms. 90.
Only once in many millions of eons does a Buddha, a Great Sage who benefits the world, appear.
That most excellent opportunity has now been obtained; abandon negligence today if you desire liberation. 91.
Rāṣṭrapāla, there are these four persons whom a bodhisattva should not associate with.
What are the four?
Rāṣṭrapāla, a person who is a bad friend (pāpamitra) is one whom a bodhisattva should not associate with.
Rāṣṭrapāla, a person who holds the view of apprehension should not be associated with by a bodhisattva.
Rāṣṭrapāla, a person who rejects the true Dharma should not be associated with by a bodhisattva.
Rāṣṭrapāla, a person who is greedy for material things should not be associated with by a bodhisattva.
Rāṣṭrapāla, these four types of persons should not be associated with by a bodhisattva.

Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses: "Those who avoid evil friends and always cultivate virtuous friends, they constantly increase on the paths to awakening, like the orb of the moon in the sky during the bright fortnight. (92)

Those who always abide in the view of apprehension, and likewise in the notions of a self, a living being, or a soul—those who seek the wisdom of the Buddha should always avoid them as they would a jar of poison. (93)

Those who reject the Dharma of the Supreme Men—which is peaceful, free from passion, and conducive to the deathless—one who desires to awaken to supreme enlightenment should avoid them just as one avoids a jar of excrement. (94)

Those who are deeply attached to food, robes, and alms bowls, and who are always intent upon intimacy with families—one should not associate with them; indeed, one should avoid them just as one would a pit of fire. 95.

Indeed, by one who desires to overcome Māra, to set in motion the supreme, unsurpassed wheel, and to thus accomplish such vast benefit for sentient beings, even that person must avoid evil friends. (96)
Having abandoned both the pleasant and the unpleasant, gain, fame, strife, pride, and envy—one who desires to awaken to supreme enlightenment should constantly seek the wisdom of a Buddha. (97)
(RP 132) Rāṣṭrapāla, there are these four dharmas that result in suffering for bodhisattvas.
What are the four?

Rāṣṭrapāla, the state of conceit regarding one's knowledge is a phenomenon that results in the maturation of suffering for bodhisattvas. Rāṣṭrapāla, a mind of envy and stinginess is a phenomenon that results in the maturation of suffering for bodhisattvas. Rāṣṭrapāla, lack of resolute faith is a phenomenon that results in the maturation of suffering for bodhisattvas.
Rāṣṭrapāla, the pursuit of enjoyment through impure knowledge and patience is a phenomenon that results in the ripening of suffering for bodhisattvas.
Rāṣṭrapāla, these are the phenomena that result in the ripening of suffering for bodhisattvas.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Those who are upholders of the Dharma on this earth are honored throughout all worlds; yet the ignorant one treats them with contempt."
By that, he encounters endless suffering. // 98 //
He always desires and delights in impure enjoyments and teaches through improper means;
he is perpetually puffed up with pride, yet bows down before teachers and noble persons. // 99 //

There is no faith in the Buddha, nor is there faith in the Dharma or the Saṅgha for that one; there is no faith in the trainings or the ascetic virtues for that evil-minded one who faces the three lower realms. (100)
Falling from here among humans due to the power of karma, being ignorant and deluded, he indeed undergoes suffering in the hells, in the animal realms, and in the states of hungry ghosts. 101.

He whose wisdom is a lamp for the world on earth, the hero among men who brings an end to the destruction of suffering—he, having abandoned the path to the lower realms, must constantly cultivate the path to enlightenment. 102.
Rāṣṭrapāla, there are these four bondages of bodhisattvas.
What are the four?
Disparaging others is a bondage of bodhisattvas.

Rāṣṭrapāla, for bodhisattvas, the perception of signs associated with the application of cultivation by worldly means is a bondage. Rāṣṭrapāla, for a bodhisattva whose mind is not restrained and who lacks wisdom, the indulgence in negligence is a bondage.
Rāṣṭrapāla, for a bodhisattva whose mind is attached, intimacy with families is a bondage.
Rāṣṭrapāla, these are the four bonds of bodhisattvas.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"He constantly despises others and always cultivates worldly meditation;
he is bound by those hundreds of views, like a weak-bodied elephant stuck in the mud. (103)

But he who is bound by attachment to family and social circles, who is always heedless and possesses a grasping mind, who is devoid of wisdom and dull-witted—he is fettered by these improper conducts. (104)

For whoever desires liberation from the fears of suffering, such as birth, old age, death, and the rest, should abandon both self-contempt and pride, and constantly apply themselves to the path to awakening. 105.

Having endured all suffering without exception to its very end, having become indifferent to all pleasure, and having abandoned every beloved and unloved kinsman without remainder, the steadfast ones, free from defilement, become Buddhas. 106.
One should apply oneself to the six qualities of the stages, to the powers, the faculties, and knowledge;
endowed always with all virtues, one shall become a Buddha, liberated from the cage of old age. (107)
For inconceivable eons, while practicing the former conduct for the benefit of sentient beings, he practiced for supreme enlightenment;
he was always well-established in generosity, self-restraint, and discipline, having renounced his kinsmen. (108)
I have always delighted in remote forests, having dried up my physical basis for the sake of awakening;
never have I slackened in vigor while seeking the wisdom of the Great Beings.

Having seen sentient beings wandering in delusion within the prison of existence in this world, you previously cultivated vast compassion here for the sake of the world, through the power of the awakening you had attained. (110)

In the past, they abandoned daughters, sisters, sons, and beloved wives, as well as abundant wealth, grain, life, cherished things, and highly prosperous lands, seeking supreme enlightenment for many eons. (111)
In that forest, which was beautiful and abundant with fruits, flowers, and water, I lived as a sage devoted to forbearance;
though my hands and feet were severed by the wicked King Kali, even then my mind was not at all corrupted.
There was an aged sage named Śyāmaka living in a forest glade; though struck by King Bharata with a firm arrow, his mind was not at all corrupted. (113)
As I cast off my body from the mountain slope for the sake of a well-spoken word, my regard was fixed upon awakening; thus, there was no concern for my body nor for my life. (114)

Having sacrificed her own body to satisfy even the tiger cubs for the sake of their lives, the tigress roared in the sky; the hosts of gods cried out, "Well done, O Great Being of steadfast heroism! (115)

And when, O young man, while wandering through previous existences, you were devoted to extreme generosity, you dried up the ocean for the sake of jewels; having obtained the gem, you brought happiness to sentient beings. (116)
When I was wandering as Sutasoma, lord of the earth, my fame being renowned,
I swiftly liberated a hundred kings who had been led to execution by means of skillful stratagems.
Seeing a man who was suffering and poor, I even gave up my own beloved body;
having obtained wealth, he was made rich by me through that virtuous King Sarvadada.
Having seen the dove who had come for refuge, the virtuous king here cut flesh from his own body and gave it; even though his own body was offered, he did not abandon the one afflicted by fear. 119.

In the past, when I was the King of Lions, having first acquired an incomparable medicine that had been gathered by physicians, I gave it away for the sake of another, even at the cost of my own life. (120)

And formerly, while practicing for the sake of the world, O Madri, you who were devoted to your husband abandoned your children; even your daughter was disregarded when you were the king’s son Sudaṃṣṭra in the presence of the assembly of monks. (121)
For a full thousand years, I endured eighty-four difficult austerities;
when my vigor was blazing, I formerly possessed even the glory of wealth and purpose.
O son of a king, Vimalatejas, with supreme devotion my body blazed before the stūpas containing the relics of the Jinas, and worship was performed for those who possess the ten powers. 123.
And Raudrākṣa, having become enraged, likewise begged for my head;
and when I was Candraprabha, O King, I cut it off and gave it to him. (124)
In all villages and cities, at the openings of every street, I established sublime medicines for the sake of sentient beings; and when that occurred, I became equal to merit itself.
When I was the auspicious King Śubha in former births, I gave away a thousand beautiful women whose bodies were adorned with gold and pearls. (126)
With excellent flowers and perfumes, and with the splendor of the finest gold and pearls, my crown was formerly offered by me when I was King Ratnacūḍa. (127)
In the past, my two hands and feet—soft as fine cotton wool, delicate as tender lotus petals, and possessed of fortitude by that king—were sacrificed. (128)
O caravan leader Siṃhala, when you were on Badara Island, you subdued hundreds of merciless, cruel, powerful, and fierce ogresses and turned them into human beings. (129)
O fool, that Rākṣasī named Pramada has her mind infatuated with sensual pleasures;
you shall liberate the five hundred merchants when you become Sunetra. 130.
Having abandoned forty million women whose forms were like those of apsarases, Puṇyaraśmi went forth into homelessness when he was under the teaching of the Jina. (131)
O King, when I was of golden complexion, my fingers were webbed, radiant, stainless, and pure, as I practiced for the sake of the welfare of beings with great generosity. (132)
O King, when she had eyes like blue lotuses, a complexion as beautiful as a blue lotus, and was lovely to the heart—delightful to the eyes—she was abandoned by me for the sake of the world. (133)
O Keśava, when I was the King of Physicians, I saw a woman struck by separation from her beloved, her beauty, mind, and dress ruined; she was liberated by my compassion. 134.
O All-Seeing One, when I was a being in a former life, seeing a man afflicted by disease, I gave my own blood; he was made free from illness by me. (135)
Having extracted my own bone from my body, marrow was given by me to one emaciated by disease;
yet never was a being abandoned by me when I was the king named Kusuma. (136)
Having renounced even his entire treasury and his own dear and beloved life, he liberated a man who had fallen into calamity, when the King previously attained the fulfillment of his purpose. (137)

O King, when he was Āśuketu, desiring awakening for the sake of the world, his pair of hands were marked with wheels, resembled lotuses, and were generous, intoxicated [with virtue], and free from worldly concern. (138)

O King, when I was all-seeing, compassionate, and desirous of the welfare and benefit of living beings, I renounced even the four continents, which were filled with prosperous men and hundreds of cities. (139)
When you were the princess Jñānavatī, having cut off your own soft, delicate, and slightly pale thigh, you joyfully and delightedly gave your own flesh and blood to me. 140.

When a woman, seeing my two breasts— golden-hued, plump, delicate, and dear to her heart— abandoned by me as I was afflicted by hunger and thirst, thought, "She has become like a mere silver [image]," she became a woman [of that name]. (141)
Exquisite and most delightful ornaments, various jewels, garments, chariots, and vehicles—many things difficult to abandon were renounced by me when I was the renowned King Viśrutaśrī. (142)
The king’s son was indeed ungrateful, yet he was rescued from the ocean; though my eye was taken for the sake of the jewels, my mind was not at all angry.
"Even when I had abandoned my excellent refuge and disregarded it, may there be no killing of ants for me; nor did my mind waver then, when I was a lizard in previous lives. (144)
Delighting in the honor of attending to others, I was always devoted to serving the elders;
even while wandering about, Kapiṃjala was never conceited nor arrogant toward men. (145)
And for the sake of one who had come for refuge, I, having generated compassion, sacrificed my body;
yet even when struck by an arrow by a hunter while in the form of a monkey, I did not abandon him. (146)

Even though my body was emaciated by being under the control of the elephant, I did not eat delicious food while remembering the world’s aged elders; it was only when I had liberated the elephant that I did so. (147)

I was the lord of bears in a mountain fastness when, struck by snow for seven days, I was protected by that man; though he employed a killer against me, I did not offer any resistance to him at that time. (148)
There was once an elephant, white as a jasmine flower, who had taken refuge in supreme awakening and sought the qualities of a Buddha;
though pierced by a poisoned arrow, he felt no hatred even while casting off his noble tusks.
In the island of Khaṇḍaka, a young partridge dwelling in the forest lived in the abode of loving-kindness;
upon merely seeing him, the fire was extinguished, and the hosts of gods scattered flowers. (150)

When I was being carried away by the waters of the Ganges' waves while in the state of a deer, I was rescued by him; because of that, my executioners were removed, yet my mind was not at all corrupted therein. (151)

Five hundred merchants, helpless and caught in the midst of the ocean, were rescued by me; even when I was born as a tortoise, I was compassionate toward them when they were hungry and about to devour me. (152)

While practicing the conduct of awakening in the past, when I was a fish dwelling in the water, I gave up my own body for the benefit of sentient beings and was devoured by hundreds of thousands of living creatures. (153)
O gentle one, when you beheld the world struck by hundreds of diseases, you raised it up;
at that time, O Prāṇaka, the beings were made happy and free from illness. 154.

When I was the lion, the king of beasts, endowed with power and strength and possessed of compassion, my mind was not corrupted even when pierced by an arrow; at that time, I maintained loving-kindness (maitrī) even toward the killer. (155)
Formerly, on the shore of the ocean, I was the king of horses, white as a conch shell or frost;
out of compassion and pity, I rescued my merchants when they were surrounded by rākṣasīs. (156)
While practicing the conduct of awakening for the sake of beings, I was once a bird named Kuṇāla;
though I avoided the many faults of the qualities of sensual desire, I did not fall under the power of women. (157)
There was once a hare living in a forest thicket who governed that troop of hares with righteousness;
while he was thus ruling, I, a sage dwelling in a hermitage, being afflicted by hunger, abandoned my own refuge for his sake. (158)

There was a parrot whose tree was once rich with flowers and fruit; though it became a withered tree, I did not abandon it. O Grateful One, Śakra saw this and then made that tree rich with leaves and fruit once again. (159)
O King of Monkeys, when I was once a monkey, I saw my troop harassed by a lordly elephant and abandoned their region; out of fear of the king, they were liberated by me. 160.
"O parrot, in the past you were seized by a man while stealing rice for the sake of your teacher.
Why then, O parrot, do you steal my rice? You are destroying even the grain [matsasyam] of the birds! (161)
The parrot said: "O good sir, listen; I do not steal your rice out of a desire for theft.
I take the rice only for the sake of supporting my two aged parents, out of compassion for them. (162)
When I first scatter the seeds, I shall give a portion of them to all people; and having heard my words as I speak them, they shall never commit theft on account of that. (163)
"Excellent, parrot! Take as much rice as you wish, for such devotion is rare even among humans.
Since you, a human, have come here to me who am an animal, may there be for you excellent self-control, tranquility, and restraint. (164)
While practicing such deeds as these in the past, performing difficult austerities, no weariness arose in my mind as I sought this supreme, stainless enlightenment. (165)
Indeed, there is no thing—whether internal or external—that has not been given by me;
I have practiced ethical discipline, patience, as well as vigor, meditation, skillful means, and wisdom. (166)
I gave my flesh, skin, marrow, and even my blood from my own body;
and finally, as I wandered, even my physical frame was withered away in mountain caves.
The vehicles of ascetic purification were taught by the Victors; by applying oneself to them, one becomes a Victor.
Therefore, while practicing in the past, I was always constantly engaged in ascetic purification.
Having heard of these noble vows which were practiced by me while I was wandering, and having heard of this marvel of theirs, my desire for them will not remain even for a single moment.
Upon hearing this very teaching at that time, they will find it laughable; devoted to food and sexual pleasure, they will be constantly overcome by sloth and full of hundreds of desires. (170)
Those who hate the Dharma are always ignoble, corrupters of the teaching, and devoid of virtue;
having heard this peaceful Dharma, they declare, "This was not spoken by the Jina. (171)
My teacher was an ocean of learning, possessed of great erudition and the best of preachers;
yet even he rejected this, for it is in no way the word of the Buddha.
In the past, there was also an elder who was his teacher, one whose flood of virtues had been fully mastered;
even by him this [teaching] was not accepted. Therefore, do not apply yourself to that which is false.

Where neither a self nor a living being is taught, and even a person (pudgala) does not exist in any way, then the exertion here—namely the practice of ethical discipline and the performance of restraint—is rendered futile. (174)
If indeed there is a Mahāyāna, yet herein there is no self, no sentient being, nor any human;
then the effort I have exerted here is in vain, since neither a self nor a sentient being is to be found. (175)
O Jina, you have never spoken these words of reproach against monks—words that are merely the fabrications of those with evil minds and the doctrines of false teachers. (176)

Shameless, lacking a sense of propriety, and of immoral conduct—like crows, bold, arrogant, and fierce—they will indeed exist here within my teaching, O monks, consumed by envy, pride, and conceit. (177)

Shaking their hands, feet, and the corners of their robes, with saffron-colored garments draped around their necks, they wander among the families of villages, intoxicated by the pride of liquor. // 178 //
Having taken up the banner of the Buddha, those servants among the householders constantly carry his letter, having abandoned the mass of virtues that bestows the teaching. 179.
Indeed, from the gift of cattle, donkeys, horses, and livestock, there arises servitude for them;
and those noble ones are constantly engaged in agriculture, trade, and the application of capital. (180)

Not even an ignoble word should be spoken to them, nor is there anything whatsoever that they should not do; for to them, wealth belonging to a stūpa, to the Saṅgha, or even personal property, is all the same. (181)
Having observed a monk who is rich in virtues, they speak ill even of him; entering as immoral, deceitful, and hypocritical ones, these most terrible beings indeed bring ruin to women. (182)
Just as householders are greedy for sensual pleasures, so too shall those who have gone forth be greedy;
they will have wives, sons, and daughters, and in these respects they will be equal to householders. (183)
In whichever family they are honored with the enjoyment of robes and alms-food, there they become greedy for wives, following the power of the afflictions, and are always ignoble. (184)

Indeed, these sensual pleasures should not be indulged in, for they cause one to fall among animals, hungry ghosts, and in the hells; and those householders will always speak [of them], while they themselves remain unsubdued and unpacified. (185)
Just as they themselves are undisciplined, their assembly of disciples will also not be well-disciplined; day and night will pass for them in talk of food and sexual intercourse. (186)
They indeed bestow their favor for the sake of service alone, and not for the sake of [my] qualities;
surrounded by my own hosts of disciples, I am always honored here among people—O moving one, attain success! 187.
They say: "This gathering of people is for my compassion toward them; I never request service from those groups of disciples. (188)
There, many overcome by disease—lepers with mottled limbs and very deformed—those who are perpetually ignoble, having arrived again and again from the hells, will go forth [into homelessness]. (189)
Devoid of the vows prescribed by the precepts, they are always separated from the qualities of a monk;
they are neither householders nor monks, being discarded like wood in a cemetery. (190)
They will have no regard for the trainings, nor for the Prātimokṣa discipline; unrestrained and acting according to their own whims, they will be like lordly elephants freed from the goad. // 191 //
For even though they dwell in the forest, their minds will be drawn toward the village;
for those fallen into the fire of the afflictions, their minds will find no stability.

Having forgotten all the qualities of the Buddha, as well as the trainings, the ascetic practices, and the skillful means, they— filled with intoxication, pride, and arrogance— fall into the terrible Avīci hell.
Constantly delighting in talk of kings and devoted to recounting stories of thieves, they are intent on attending to their kinsmen, brooding over them day and night. (194)

Having abandoned meditation as well as study, they are constantly engaged in the affairs of the monastery; greedy for their dwellings, they are surrounded by disciples who are themselves unsubdued. // 195 //
"I am not a laborer in this monastery; indeed, it was built by me for my own sake.
There is space in the monastery for those monks who are favorable toward me. (196)

Those who possess morality and virtuous qualities, who uphold the Dharma and are dedicated to the welfare of beings, and who are constantly engaged in self-control and restraint—you do not show them any gathering [of followers]. (197)
"This dwelling has been assigned to me, and this one to my co-resident; this one is for my companion in joy. Go, for there is no place here for you to stay. (198)
"All bedding and seats have been given away; many monks have been established here.
There is no possibility of gain here; what will you consume? Go from here, O monk! (199)
Furthermore, they will never even designate beds or seats; they will become accumulators of household goods, possessing abundant possessions and retinues. // 200 //
Even when rebuked by me from all sides, those sons of mine in the final age do not heed my words; instead, they dwell then in remote forests.
Alas! Before long, the teaching of the Supreme Victor will indeed perish, neglected by many monks who have become overwhelmed by gain and hostile toward virtue. (202)
And those endowed with the virtues of ethical discipline will be constantly despised during the final age;
they shall dwell in forests and wildernesses, having abandoned villages, kingdoms, and cities. (203)
Those who are devoid of virtue, divisive, slanderous, and fond of quarreling will always be honored; though despised by the Teacher, they will be consumed by pride and arrogance. // 204 //

This teaching, a treasury of virtues, possessing the form of all excellences and supremely delightful, shall not go to ruin here through my failure in ethical discipline or the faults of envy and pride. (205)
Just as a jewel-mine becomes depleted or a lotus-pond becomes parched, so too, when the sacrificial pillar made of the finest jewels is broken, the Teaching will perish in the final age. (206)
In this final age, there will occur a most terrible destruction of the Dharma;
and those undisciplined monks shall be the destroyers of this teaching of mine. (207)

For those who are not devoted to practicing the conduct [of the bodhisattvas], there is no association with them anywhere; indeed, when they pass away from this life, their destination is that of hungry ghosts, residence even in hell, or the realm of animals. (208)
Having experienced intense and bitter suffering for many hundreds of infinite years,
even if he attains a human birth, he is born miserable and constantly pitiable. (209)
One who constantly practices this evil conduct is born blind, deaf, or one-eyed, with variegated limbs and extremely deformed; he is loathsome in appearance and terrifying to behold. (210)
No one places confidence in him, nor do they have faith in his words; he is constantly reviled by all who practice an uneven course of conduct. (211)
Tormented by hundreds of diseases and sufferings, struck by blows from clods of earth and wooden staves, they are consumed by hunger and thirst, and are always utterly humiliated. (212)
Knowing that sufferings are endless, abandon the practice of evil from afar; always cultivate virtuous conduct, lest you experience regret hereafter. 213

For one who holds dear the Buddha, the noble assembly, the training, and the ascetic qualities (dhutadharma), one should constantly apply oneself in this way, having abandoned kin, gain, fame, and renown. 214.

For this conditioned world is like an illusion, difficult to traverse, and equal to a dream; it is not to be relied upon, for before long there will be separation from all that is dear, for nothing here is eternal. 215
Exert yourselves and strive constantly in the perfections, the stages, and the powers; never let your vigor falter until you awaken to supreme enlightenment. 216.
The First Chapter: The Introduction.
The Second Chapter.
Rāṣṭrapāla, for the most part, these faults will arise among persons belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle: those who are not diligent will honor those who are not diligent;
the deceitful will honor the deceitful.
The ignorant will consider the ignorant worthy of honor;
they will be fond of worldly gain.
Abounding in attachment, they will be envious of families, deceitful, like crows, talkative, fraudulent, and will hold the warrior class in high esteem.
They will procure gain by speaking of one another's virtues;
and they will enter villages for the sake of seeking gain,
not for the sake of maturing sentient beings, nor out of compassion for sentient beings.
Those ignorant ones will claim themselves to be for the sake of knowledge, thinking, "How might others know me as one who is deeply learned and possessed of virtuous qualities?
And they will become disrespectful, just like those who have not applied themselves to practice.
They will become like broken vessels, seeking out one another's faults;
they will have lost their application, being ignorant, lazy, and lacking wisdom, full of new fabrications.

Through their discordant recitation of the Dharma, they will follow their own whims, harbor deep enmity, and be filled with malice. Under the guise of instructing others through improper reproaches, they will conduct themselves within this teaching, being by nature unwilling to inquire.
Having no interest in hearing the Dharma,
they will take rebirth in poor families due to their improper conduct;
having gone forth in these poor families, they will find satisfaction in this teaching through mere gain alone.
For them there will be no confession of transgressions, much less the realization of knowledge;
having cast aside the qualities of a Buddha, they will claim for themselves the status of "monks" merely by the acquisition of renown.
Rāṣṭrapāla, I do not say that such individuals possess even conformable patience, much less the wisdom of a Buddha; for them,
a happy rebirth is far away.
What, then, is awakening?
Furthermore, Rāṣṭrapāla, for such persons as these, I declare eight qualities that create obstacles to awakening.
What are the eight?

Rebirth in the lower realms, rebirth in a poor family, rebirth in a border region, rebirth in a low caste, being ill-favored, blindness, and other such conditions, association with evil friends, being highly conceited, and dying without having avoided dangerous circumstances— Rāṣṭrapāla, I declare these eight factors to be obstacles to awakening.
For what reason?
Rāṣṭrapāla, I do not say that one who makes a verbal vow attains awakening;
nor do I say that one who is deceitful possesses purity of conduct.
I do not speak of the practice of awakening for the deceitful; I do not speak of worshiping the Buddha for one who values material gain;
I do not speak of the purification of wisdom for the conceited.
I do not say that one who is possessed of poor wisdom can sever doubt; I do not say that one who is stingy can achieve purity of intention;
I do not say that one who lacks abundant resolute faith can attain dhāraṇī.

I do not say that one who seeks out false virtues will attain a happy rebirth; I do not say that one who is stingy regarding their family lineage will achieve purity of body; I do not say that one who has not cultivated the noble path will encounter the Buddhas.

I do not speak of purity of speech for one who is attached to family; I do not speak of purity of mind for one who lacks reverence; I do not speak of a desire for the Dharma for one who does not know moderation.
I do not speak of the pursuit of the Dharma for one who is attached to body and life.
Rāṣṭrapāla, I do not censure those six teachers as much as I censure those deluded men.
Why is that?
Speaking one way and acting another, they are deceivers of the world including the devas.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:

"Those who are unrestrained, restless, and arrogant; those who lack respect, are conceited, and obsessed with gain; those overcome by afflictions, fickle, and full of worldly attachments—such as these are very far from supreme enlightenment. (217)
For one overcome by gain, laziness increases; for one who has become lazy, faith is destroyed.
For one whose faith is ruined, ethical discipline is destroyed; for one who has become immoral, good association is destroyed. // 218 //
For those who, having been poor, went forth into homelessness and attained honor that frees one from poverty, have—as if casting off a burden of gold—taken up again that burden of grain. (219)
Seeking gain, he enters the forest; having gone there, he searches for kin.
Abandoning the perfections of supernormal knowledge, spells, and eloquence, he instead embraces his relatives. (220)

Under the influence of pride, those deluded ones take birth in the realms of misery, in unfavorable states, in poverty, and in low-born families; they also incur blindness from birth, weakness, and a lack of physical vigor. (221)

Having fallen away from the practice of their proper conduct, their mindfulness lost through the acquisition of negligence, they will fall into a terrible, great abyss from which there is no liberation even in ten million eons. // 222 //
If one could obtain enlightenment here through gain, then even Devadatta would obtain enlightenment;
just as a bird is carried away by a whirlwind, so too are those who are undisciplined swept away by gain.

Devoid of merit, greedy for the wives of others, and impure in conduct, they are obstructed from wholesome qualities; in the teaching, they are like wood in a cemetery that causes harm—those who have not attained wisdom through the thought of awakening (bodhicitta). 224.

One who seeks awakening searches for the qualities of a Buddha and does not remain as one who has attained liberation; the awakening of one overcome by pride is just like a monkey made firm by being smeared with pitch. (225)
Even by me, seeking enlightenment, my own dear life was sacrificed for the sake of a single word of the Dharma.
But those who have abandoned the Dharmas and are unyoked from yoga—having become useless—they fall away from the Teaching. (226)
In former times, for the sake of the meaning of the well-spoken word, I fell into a great abyss ablaze with fire;
having heard it, I remained established in its practice, abandoning all that is pleasant and unpleasant. (227)
Having heard of their manifold teachings rich in virtue, even a desire for them does not arise in a single moment.
How can there be awakening for one who desires unrighteousness? It is just like showing the way to a blind man. (228)
Thus it is said.

Once upon a time, Rāṣṭrapāla, in the past, incalculable, more than incalculable, inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, vast, and infinite eons ago, there appeared in the world a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Siddhārthabuddhi— one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans.
And there was the Buddha, the Blessed One. At that time, O Rāṣṭrapāla, there was a king named Arciṣmān;
the kingdom of King Arciṣmān in Jambūdvīpa extended for sixteen thousand yojanas.

And at that time, Rāṣṭrapāla, there were twenty thousand cities in that Jambudvīpa, all of which contained thousands of millions of households. Furthermore, Rāṣṭrapāla, King Arciṣmān had a capital city named Ratnaprabhāsa where he resided; it was twelve yojanas in length from east to west.
It was seven yojanas in extent from south to north,
and it was well-constructed with seven walls made of the seven precious gems and eightfold crossroads.
At that time, the lifespan of sentient beings was ten billion nayutas of years.
Furthermore, Rāṣṭrapāla, King Arciṣmān had a son named Puṇyaraśmi, who was handsome, pleasing, and beautiful to behold, endowed with an excellence of most sublime complexion.
As soon as he was born, a thousand treasuries appeared;
and within the king’s palace, one treasury consisting of the seven precious gems appeared, measuring ten men in height.
Furthermore, Rāṣṭrapāla, as soon as Prince Puṇyaraśmi was born, all the beings of Jambudvīpa became joyful;
and those beings who were in bondage were released from their bonds.
Moreover, Rāṣṭrapāla, within seven days, that Prince Puṇyaraśmi mastered all worldly arts and crafts, however many there may be.
Then, Rāṣṭrapāla, at the hour of midnight, the deities belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host exhorted Prince Puṇyaraśmi: "O Prince, you must always be heedful;
you must be skilled in contemplating impermanence.
For the life of human beings, O Prince, is indeed short."
The future life must be traversed;
therefore, you should be one who perceives the fear of the world beyond, and not one who is negligent in performing wholesome deeds.
At that time, he spoke these verses:
O Prince, do not be utterly heedless; do not fall under the power of negligence.
Heedfulness has been praised by the Sugata, for those who are heedless have been censured by the Sugatas. (229)

Those who are heedful in this world, gentle, delighting in generosity and self-restraint, free from envy, and whose minds are filled with compassion and loving-kindness toward all beings—they soon become the supreme among men. // 230 //
Those immeasurable Sugatas who have passed away, those who exist now, and indeed those yet to come—
all have risen through their roots of virtue and are firmly established upon the very path of heedfulness.
Food, drink, clothing, and ornaments of gold, silver, and jewels were given by them for tens of millions of eons, as they sought supreme enlightenment here. (232)
When asked for their hands, feet, ears, or noses, they give them away with great joy;
with their intentions fulfilled by all the qualities of enlightenment, they will before long become the best of men. // 233 //

Having completely abandoned the pleasures, power, and wealth of sovereignty, as well as beloved wives— who are like an illusion on a stage— take refuge in the forest alone, free from all desire, for this conditioned world is like a theatrical performance.
Life is always flickering and unstable, like a clay pot destined to break;
it is transient, like something borrowed, and never permanent. O youth, there is nothing auspicious here, for it is always impure. (235)
Neither mother, nor father, nor kinsmen can prevent one from falling into an evil state when one strives [toward it];
for whatever good or evil has been done follows after one at the time of death. (236)
For the sake of desire, throughout many oceans of eons, you have been killed by one another in vain;
you have not brought benefit to anyone, and your exertion has been entirely fruitless. (237)
Today you seek for this world the incomparable peace of enlightenment, the supreme state; though even your marrow, flesh, and skin may wither away, do not let yourself become weary. (238)
For the appearance of a Sugata is rare, and hearing the peaceful Dharma is very difficult to obtain;
having diligently shaken off the faction of Māra, you shall before long attain the wisdom of a Buddha. 239.
Always attend upon virtuous friends and forever avoid evil companions; they lead you ever onto the true path and constantly restrain you from the wrong path. (240)

Having exerted firm and excellent vigor, and having abandoned all longing for body and life, with hearts as steadfast as adamant and a firm foundation, [follow] this very well-heard path of the Buddha. (241)

For indeed, this supreme and unsurpassed state is difficult to attain; all the former Best of Men were devoted to dwelling in the forest and were illuminators. You should follow their path and practice accordingly. 242.

Always be devoted to dwelling in the forest; having abandoned beloved mothers, sons, fathers, and kinsmen, as well as all your friends and even the craving for body and life, seek today this vast accumulation of the Sugata’s wisdom, seeking indeed that supreme, unsurpassed state. 243.
Then, Rāṣṭrapāla, from that time forward for ten years, Prince Puṇyaraśmi never succumbed to sloth or torpor;
he never laughed, nor did he play or take pleasure.
He never indulged in pleasures, nor did he ever go to garden grounds; he was never amazed upon seeing his companions, nor did he ever become desirous of song.
He never conceived a longing for sovereignty, wealth, houses, or cities.

Thus he became indifferent toward all things; remaining alone, lost in thought, he stayed in seclusion, contemplating the state of extreme frailty and losing confidence in this world as being essence-less and transient.

"Encountering the unpleasant, separation from the beloved, deceiving the foolish, the lack of flavor in delighting in *saṃsāra*, the joy of sovereignty which is subject to destruction, the constant hostility of the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who is never satisfied with tranquility—
I am now in the midst of fools and unrighteous people; what if I were to pass my time in silence?"
Remaining alone in a secluded place, silent and reflecting upon heedfulness, he dwelt solitary, contemplating separation from what is dear.
Then, Rāṣṭrapāla, King Arciṣmān had a city named Ratipradhāna constructed on a certain spot of earth for the prince’s enjoyment.

It measured seven hundred streets from south to north and was surrounded on all sides by seven walls made of the seven precious substances, which were draped with networks of tinkling bells, pearl lattices, and canopies of jeweled poles.
And at all the entrances to the streets, eighty thousand jeweled pillars were erected;
upon every jeweled pillar, thousands of jeweled cords were fastened;
and everywhere along those jeweled cords, fourteen billion rows of palm trees were attached.
When stirred by the wind and struck together by the wind, they produced a sound like that of a hundred thousand musical instruments.

At every street entrance, five hundred maidens had been stationed—skilled in singing, skilled in dancing, having reached the prime of youth, and available for the enjoyment of all the world. King Arciṣmān gave them this command: "Day and night, you must engage in no other discourse except for dancing, singing, and instrumental music."
All those who come from the four directions should be delighted,
so that perhaps a mind of joy might arise in the prince; nor should anything unpleasant be said to any living being.
Furthermore, at all those street entrances, food was given to those seeking food, drink to those seeking drink,
vehicles to those seeking vehicles, and even clothing, perfumes, garlands, ointments, beds, dwellings, and the necessities of life.
Gold, silver, gems, pearls, beryl, conch-shells, stones, coral, gold, silver, elephants, horses, and refined ornaments—all these were established as heaps of jewels for the enjoyment of all people.

At that time, a palace one *yojana* in circumference was constructed around the center of the city for the prince’s use; it was laid out like a chessboard with the seven precious gems and adorned with seven archways.
And there a palace was constructed,
wherein forty million couches were prepared for the prince’s use.
And in its center a garden was laid out, which was completely filled and covered with every kind of flowering tree, every kind of fruit tree, and every kind of jewel tree.
Furthermore, Rāṣṭrapāla, in the center of that park a lotus pond was constructed, made of the seven precious gems and featuring stairways of four jewels—
namely, gold, silver, beryl, and crystal.
And there were one hundred and eight lion-mouths through which scented water entered that very lotus pond.

There were exactly eight hundred lion-faced spouts through which that water flowed out again. That lotus pond was perpetually and constantly filled with blue, red, yellow, and white lotuses; it was surrounded on all sides by jewel trees and strewn with trees bearing flowers and fruits in all seasons.
On the bank of that pond, eight hundred jewel trees had been planted.
Upon every jewel-tree, sixty-six jeweled cords were fastened; and everywhere, millions of rows of palm trees were fixed.
When these were stirred by the wind and struck together by the wind, a sound issued forth, just like that of hundreds of thousands of musical instruments being played in concert.
And that lotus pond was covered with a network of jewels above,
so that no dust or dirt might fall upon the prince's body.
And at that time, forty million seats made of the seven precious gems had been arranged in that palace. On every seat, five hundred pieces of fine cloth were spread.
And in the center of that place, a seat made of the seven precious gems was arranged, seven men’s heights in height, and covered with eighty million pieces of fine cloth.
Wherever Prince Puṇyaraśmi was to sit,
at every seat a censer of agallochum incense was burned.
Three times during the day and three times during the night, a bed of flowers was prepared.
It was covered with a golden canopy, hung with golden lotuses, spread with a net of pearls, and illuminated by the radiance of precious jewels; eighty thousand [pendants] were suspended from it.
And upon every jeweled tree, hundreds of banners were hung.
Throughout the entire park, ninety million jewel-gems with a radiance extending for a yojana were established,
and by their light, the entire world was illuminated.
Furthermore, Rāṣṭrapāla, in that park there were birds such as parrots, mainas, cranes, cuckoos, peacocks, swans, ruddy geese, kunālas, kalaviṅkas, and jīvañjīvakas, which spoke with human voices.
From the warbling of those birds crying out in the Nandana grove, a sound as intoxicating as that of the gods issued forth.
And for the prince’s enjoyment, five hundred varieties of food of the five tastes were constantly and perpetually prepared, perfect in every respect.

Furthermore, at that time, twenty thousand young men—having passed their sixteenth year—were gathered from all the cities and brought into that city; eighty million who were skilled in the methods of all arts and crafts and skilled in the methods of all worldly pleasures and requisites were brought into that city.
Ten million maidens were given to him by his parents.
Ten million maidens were given by the assembly of kinsmen, ten million by the merchants and the wise, and ten million by Sarvarāja.

And they were all beautiful, gracious, and lovely to behold; all were sixteen years of age, noble by birth, skilled in song, skilled in instrumental music, skilled in dance, skilled in laughter, and skilled in approaching men. They were upright, youthful, sweet, mature, the first to speak, with smiling faces, skilled in polite conduct, knowledgeable in the rules of all the arts, and neither too tall.
They were neither too short nor too tall, neither too fair nor too dark;
from them the fragrance of blue lotuses wafted spontaneously,
and the scent of sandalwood issued from their limbs.
Like manifest celestial maidens, they moved with exclusive and flawless grace;
and the prince Puṇyaraśmi, standing in their midst, was there amidst the sound of that music by means of its resonant melody.
And he generates this thought: "Alas! This great host of enemies has appeared before me, plundering my wholesome qualities.
