Come now, I shall be without regard for them.
At that time, he would be just like a man condemned to death who, upon seeing [his executioners], does not give rise to a mind of wonder.
In this very way, when Prince Puṇyaraśmi saw that woman, he was not astonished, nor was he astonished by that city, nor by her companions.
During those ten years, he never grasped the sign of form;
nor did he grasp the sign of sound, the sign of odor, the sign of taste, or the sign of touch.
On the contrary, he directed his mind in this way: "When, at last, will my liberation from the midst of such a host of enemies come to pass?"
"When shall I practice heedfulness so that my liberation will come about?
Then those maidens reported to King Arciṣmān: "Your Majesty, the prince does not play;
he does not take delight."
"Does he not consort with her? Then, Rāṣṭrapāla, King Arciṣmān, together with eighty thousand kings, approached the prince Puṇyaraśmi.
Having approached him, with a tearful face and a trembling body, he fell to the ground in grief.
Rising from the surface of the earth, he addressed the prince Puṇyaraśmi with these verses:
"O jewel among the best of sons, listen to my lamentation; overcome by grief, I have fallen to the ground at the end of the night.
Tell me, who has done you an unkindness? Speak! I shall inflict punishment upon him here this very instant."

Behold today my city, as delightful as a host of gods, which I have mentally fashioned for your sake. Tell me quickly what part of it is lacking today; I shall show you even the splendor of Śakra here this day. (245)
Behold this host of women, with eyes as beautiful as lotuses, afflicted by grief and lamenting like celestial nymphs.
Rejoice with them and others, casting off your sorrow; why do you brood with a dejected face as if pierced by a dart? (246)
These women are beautiful in their natural limbs, skilled in the arts of love, and possess certain knowledge of the timing of song and rhythm;
today is the time for your pleasure, not for grieving—why are you so dejected today, like a withered lotus?
With the branches of the garden trees strewn with flowers, fruits, and leaves, it is like the variegated chariot of the gods raised on high;
consider this first, for this is your prime of youth—this is the time for pleasure, so enjoy yourself here today, my son; be gracious.

This lotus pond of yours is also equal to those of the gods for the purpose of bathing; strewn with groves of blue and red lotuses and adorned with intoxicated, excellent bees, who here would not take delight in it upon reflection, my son? (249)

Swans, peacocks, parrots, mynas, and cuckoos, along with koṇālas, jīvakas, and kalaviṅkas—all possessing enchanting voices—like the Gandharvas on Mount Mādana near the Himavat; hearing these, what man here would not find delight? (250)
These Vaijayanta palaces, with their nets of pearls and crest-jewels of gems, appear as if inlaid with beryl and gold;
they possess excellent jewel-thrones covered with choice rugs, and rows of golden bracelets and palm-clappers that produce beautiful sounds.
For your sake as well, in the streets, distributions of gifts are proclaimed with the sounds of deep, steady,
and excellent musical instruments; and thousands of maidens are made to sing many songs, which are heard just like those of the apsarases in the Nandana grove.
Why, in this delightful palace equal to the third heaven, do you not take pleasure here, with your mind thus distracted? (252)
"O Prince, these companions of yours in play are equal in nature to the gods; sport with them, my son!
Your mother and father stand here with throats choked with tears; is there no sorrow, and do you have no compassion for these people? (253)

Then he, who was rich in virtues, perceiving the faults of existence, weary of conditioned things, and having no desire for the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, beheld this world trapped in the cage of saṃsāra; seeking liberation, he said to his father: "Listen, O King! (254)
No one has done me any displeasure; indeed, I have no desire for the qualities of sensual pleasure today.
For all those who are dear to me are now like enemies, devoid of affection, and they cause me to fall into the precipice of the afflictions and miserable rebirths. (255)
For these women are delightful only to the ignorant and childish; they are great precipices bound by the cords of Māra’s snares.
Since they are thus constantly censured by noble persons, why do I serve them—the very roots of hell, miserable rebirths, and sorrow? (256)
For these women are merely a deceptive facade of beauty; they are a machine of sinews and bones, impure and useless.
They are clearly like charnel grounds, leaking blood, urine, excrement, and filth—how could I take delight in them? (257)
I shall not listen to song, nor shall I take up the sound of instrumental music; let there be no delight in dreams, which are delusions for the ignorant.
O you who are greedy for mental constructions, the ignorant go to their destruction; why then shall I become like a foolish person, a slave to the afflictions? (258)

All these trees and creepers, now that the cold season has set in, have become as unattractive as trees in a wilderness; for this impermanence is the disperser of all splendor, yet through delusion I succumb to negligence while life is so fleeting. (259)
The mind, like the ocean, cannot be satiated; one who is devoted to the activity of craving will only desire more.
Beholding the world striking one another for the sake of sensual desires, may I remain as unshakable as Mount Meru by the winds. (260)
O King, you are not my father, nor my siblings, nor my wives; neither are you my savior nor my kinsmen from this misfortune.
We are all like drops of dew upon blades of grass; O Father, let us not fall under the sway of the mind and become heedless. 261.

"Alas for youth, O Lord of Men, since it is not eternal! Alas for the passing of life, as swift as mountain water! Alas for this conditioned world, flickering like lightning or a cloud! Alas, O King, for the passion of desire within the three realms of existence for one who has been tormented! (262)
I have been exhorted by the gods: "O Lord, be vigilant! A Bodhisattva does not become one who is attached to sense objects.
May you become a Buddha here, compassionate for the welfare of the world; O King of Men, there is no awakening for one whose conduct is characterized by heedlessness. (263)
O King, he who is overcome by desire is a slave to his own mind; indeed, being intent on destroying merit, he is turned away from heaven.
One should never practice sorcery, even when fueled by violence; like a bird caught in a cage, how could one find peace? 264.
The elements are like snakes and the aggregates are murderers; the mind is with outflows, useless, and empty—a village.
O Lord of Men, this body is like a poisonous tree in flower; how can I find delight in this, when it must be crossed over the flood? (265)
You behold this world fallen into evil destinies, even as the manifest state—though like the sky—is ablaze.
O King, for the sake of their liberation, I shall today swiftly assemble here the ship of the auspicious Dharma.
In order to awaken those who sleep, to sustain the lives of the afflicted, to uproot thorns, and to lead back those who have gone astray,
he proclaimed the release from bondage throughout the great trichiliocosm, satisfying those long impoverished with his sublime speech.
I shall also rescue those sinking on the path to miserable rebirths; I shall provide eyes for the blind and dry up the creeper of craving.
With the supreme lamp of liberation, whose flame is wisdom, they shall behold the three worlds as being like a theatrical stage. (268)

I shall cool the world, long tormented by heat, with clouds formed from the massed peaks of the perfections of compassion and mercy; thundering for the sake of sentient beings and garlanded with the lightning of insight, I shall bring cooling showers of the rain of bliss that carries the factors of enlightenment. 269.
Remembering this, I sit here upon the earth; I have no aspiration for any conditioned desires.
For I wander here seeking awakening for the sake of sentient beings; indeed, I have no desire at all for delight in worldly existence. (270)
Knowing this, O King, who would dwell here in the midst of enemies? What wise person would travel along a path fraught with danger?
Or who, O dear one, though possessing sight, would fall into a precipice? And having attained the path to enlightenment, who would be heedless? (271)
The entire world follows the current, but I go against that current; O King, it is not possible here for me to attain awakening through mere words.
I would rather venture into the ocean, even if it were as vast as Mount Meru, than let my mind find delight here in sensual desires.
Go quickly, O King, together with your excellent kinsmen; indeed, renounce all worldly pleasure in the kingdom throughout the entire world.
Let him take it and go wherever he desires, for my father, there is nothing in my household that I would not give, even for ten million kingdoms, provided there is no negligence on my part.
Enlightenment cannot be attained by one situated in the midst of a multitude of women—a state that is auspicious and the unsurpassed security of yoga.
I shall go and take refuge in the interior of mountains and forests; for enlightenment was indeed attained by the Victor who delighted in the wilderness.
Then, Rāṣṭrapāla, while the prince Puṇyaraśmi was still on the palace roof walking to and fro with those women, his mind became agitated, and he dwelt in only three postures.
Which three?
Standing, walking, and sitting.
Free from sloth and torpor, having ascended to the upper terrace of the palace and established himself on the eighth stage,
he heard at the hour of midnight that deities belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm were passing by, proclaiming the praises of the Buddha,
and extensively proclaiming the praises of the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
And having heard this, Rāṣṭrapāla, the prince Puṇyaraśmi, with the hairs on his body standing on end, shed tears.
Overcome by a sense of spiritual urgency, he joined his palms in reverence and addressed that deity in verses:
(Vaidya, RP 150)

"O deities, having conceived compassion for me who am suffering here, if you will not be angry, I would like to ask something. Whose virtues do you proclaim as you travel through the atmosphere? Having heard these words of mine, my mind here feels comforted. (275)

Then, Rāṣṭrapāla, those deities addressed Prince Puṇyaraśmi in verses: "O Prince, have you not heard of the Buddha, the refuge for those without refuge, named Siddhārthabuddhi? He is skilled in the conduct of others and enriched with the virtues of merit and wisdom; his Saṅgha consists of ten million times ten thousand practitioners. (276)
Puṇyarasmi said:

"O Victor, I too wish to see what his form is like; please tell me, and furthermore, what is his complexion? I also ask: what is the conduct of awakening (bodhicaryā) such that by practicing it, one becomes the sole protector of all sentient beings? (277)
Then those deities addressed Prince Puṇyaraśmi in verses:
"The hair on his head is soft, beautiful, and curls to the right; his uṣṇīṣa shines like a golden mountain peak.
His ūrṇā between the brows is as empty as the sky and as pure as a crystal gem; his navel is formed with a clockwise turn. (278)

With eyes as pure as a swarm of bees and the luster of blue lotuses, with a jaw like a lion’s and lips like the bimba fruit, this Self-Existent One (Svayambhū) emits thousands of infinite millions of rays; he vibrates throughout the three thousandfold world-system, drying up the miserable realms. // 279 //

The teeth of that most excellent and supreme Victor are equal, closely set, well-rounded, variegated, and very white—pure as snow or silver; his twenty teeth are doubled by four tusks, and his tongue is vast enough to cover his own face. // 280 //

Accompanied by the meaning of the best of mountains, gladdening to him, consistent, free from crookedness, and perfectly joined with the resonance of Brahmā; equal to the speech of a Jina or an Arhat, accompanied by hundreds of thousands of musical instruments, it pacifies wrong views and brings satisfaction to those who seek the truth. (281)

The awakening of the Victorious One is a garland of Dharma, variegated with flawless qualities and conforming to the factors of enlightenment; it is strung together like hundreds of thousands of necklaces, resounded by the joy of musical instruments, delightful with the songs of deities, possessing a voice as sweet as the radiance of the immortals, and truly gladdening. (282)

The voices of the *kinnaras*, kalaviṅkas, cuckoos, ruddy geese, peacocks, swans, and *konālaka* birds possess the resonance of Brahmā’s speech; their vocal qualities are unimpeded and faultless, leading to the realization of all meanings. (283)

Smooth as variegated crystal, pleasing to the wise, it is exhortative, disciplining, enlightening, and lovely; it is not contrary to the conduct of others, satisfying when questioned—such are the qualities of the speech of this Lord of Dharma. (284)
His neck is beautiful with its three folds, his shoulders are well-rounded and peaceful;
his arms are long like iron bars, and his body possesses the seven protuberances.
His hands are lovely and well-formed with long, rounded fingers, and the body of that Jina has the color of refined gold. 285.
His body hairs grow individually and turn to the right; his navel is deep; his private organ is concealed within a sheath like that of a horse;

his thighs are like the trunks of elephants; his shanks are like those of an antelope; he is self-arisen; and the palms of his hands are beautifully adorned with auspicious signs such as the svastika and the wheel. (286)
He who walks with the gait of a lordly elephant, strides with the prowess of a lion, and moves with the grace of a bull, has grown tall like a sacred sacrificial post.
A rain of celestial flowers falls, and flower-parasols follow him as he walks; these are the wonders of the Dharma.

In gain or loss, in pleasure or pain, in infamy or fame, and likewise in blame or praise, he is entirely unstained—like a lotus by water. Thus, in this world, there is no being equal to this Lion among Men. 288.

Then indeed, Rāṣṭrapāla, having heard the praise of the Buddha, and having heard in detail the praise of the Dharma and the Saṅgha, Prince Puṇyaraśmi became contented, elated, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and happiness.

Then, Rāṣṭrapāla, this thought occurred to the prince Puṣparśmi: "Such is the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One; such is the excellence of his Saṅgha; and such is the Dharma that has been realized by him."
Such is his excellence of disciples,
such is the cycle of existence as the encounter with sense objects, and such is the cycle of existence as being ungrateful.
Just as foolish ordinary people are ungrateful,
just as the view of a self-identity is perilous, and just as living in a household is fraught with many dangers.
Just as sensual pleasures have many faults,
just as negligence is censured by the wise,
and just as there is the darkness of ignorance consisting of delusion, so too [is this].
Just as the formative forces (saṃskāras) are difficult to penetrate,
just as the mind is difficult to tame,
and just as name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is profound, so too [is this].
Just as the six sense bases are without relish,
just as contact has suffering as its ripening when it is not fully understood,
and just as feelings have many disadvantages;
Just as craving is a tight bond,
just as clinging is difficult to relinquish,
and just as the craving for existence is ignoble;
When existence exists, there is birth which is to be utterly cut off as suffering; there is aging which causes transformation; and there is illness which causes destruction.
Just as death is devoid of delight, just as worldly engagement yields little gratification,
and just as the production of existence entails many dangers, so too [is this].

Just as the teaching of the Tathāgata is beautiful, so it cannot be purified even on the path to a happy rebirth by one who is a slave to sensual desires, deluded by the afflictions, possessed of a callous mind, delighting in negligence, dwelling among the foolish, possessing improper mental focus, whose mind is stained by cyclic existence, or who dwells among the wicked.
"How much less, then, could he possibly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?
Then this thought occurred to him: "What if I were to leap from this very palace facing the east?
Lest my host of kinsmen should create an obstacle for me as I am departing through the gate."
Then, Rāṣṭrapāla, the prince Puṇyaraśmi threw himself from that palace toward where the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Siddhārthabuddhi,
was, and spoke thus: "If that Tathāgata knows all and sees all, may the Tathāgata take heed of me."
Then, Rāṣṭrapāla, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Siddhārthabuddhi extended his right hand and emitted a radiance by which Prince Puṇyaraśmi was touched.
From that radiance there appeared a hundred-thousand-petaled lotus, as large as a chariot wheel.
And from that lotus, hundreds of thousands of rays of light issued forth,
and there was a great radiance; by that radiance, Prince Puṇyaraśmi was suffused with light.

Then, Rāṣṭrapāla, Prince Puṇyaraśmi, standing upon that lotus, extended his joined palms toward where the Blessed One Siddhārthabuddhi—the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha—was located, and uttered this inspired exclamation: "Homage to the Buddha!"
Then, Rāṣṭrapāla, that Tathāgata Siddhārthabuddhi withdrew that radiance,
and the youth fell at the feet of that Blessed One like a tree cut down at its base, and he paid homage to the Tathāgata a hundred thousand times.

Then, Rāṣṭrapāla, the prince Puṇyaraśmi addressed the Blessed One with these verses: "O King of Physicians, after a long time I have today finally obtained you, who were sought by me who have long been afflicted. Tell me, O Protector, how I, remaining steadfast, may become a recipient of the Sugata’s teaching. (289)
O Leader, I heard of heedfulness from the deities in heaven while listening at night;
having heard it, I have indeed come here in agitation, wondering how there can be heedlessness among men. (290)
Today you are the guide for me who have lost my way; today you are the eye for me who am born blind.
Lift me up from this great abyss! O you who inspire faith, you who are compassionate, you who are healers! 291.
O Protector, gather in those who have become impoverished; grant me liberation today from my bonds!
Cut through the uncertainty and wrong views of those who doubt, and explain my conduct upon the path to awakening. (292)
Show me the ford as I am being carried away; provide a lamp for me in the darkness.
For you have wounded me, so heal me free of wounds; O King of Physicians, extract the thorn from me! 293.

Having liberated me from the peril of the miserable realms, cut through my grasping at the perception of existence; carry me across to the further shore of the great flood of sorrow by means of the eightfold path, the great highway. (294)

Life is short and subject to decay; even wholesome deeds are beset by many obstacles. Yet, the fruition of merit is accomplished before long. Since I have now obtained this opportune moment, tell me with one-pointed certainty. (295)
O Lord of the World, explain this to me: how indeed may a bodhisattva be vigilant; how, by practicing the supreme conduct of awakening, may I liberate the world from the bonds of existence? (296)
Then, Rāṣṭrapāla, the Tathāgata Siddhārthabuddhi, having understood the noble intention of Prince Puṇyaraśmi, extensively proclaimed the conduct of awakening;
upon hearing this, Prince Puṇyaraśmi attained the dhāraṇī called "Liberation" and acquired the five superknowledges.
Standing in the air, he manifested flowers and scattered them over that Tathāgata, showering them down upon him.
Then, Rāṣṭrapāla, the prince Puṇyaraśmi descended from that sky and praised the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Siddhārthabuddhi, with these verses:

"I bow to you, who resemble the color of gold, endowed with excellent marks, and whose face is like the stainless moon. I bow to you, who possess unequaled wisdom; there is no one like you, free from dust, in the three worlds. (297)
O Jina, your hair is soft, beautiful, glossy, and auspicious; your uṣṇīṣa here is like the king of mountains.
There is no one equal to you in being seen with the uṣṇīṣa, and O Sage, the ūrṇā on your excellent brow shines brilliantly.

O Jina, whose excellent eyes are as beautiful as the luster of blue lotuses and white as jasmine, ivory, conch, or snow—by means of which you gaze upon this world with compassion, I pay homage to you, O one of stainless vision. 299.
Your tongue is long, slender, and copper-colored, with which you cover your own face;
speaking the Dharma, you discipline the world—I bow to you whose speech is sweet and tender. 300.
Your teeth are beautiful, very firm, and like diamonds; thirty in number, they are even and closely set.
Smiling, you discipline the world; I bow to you, whose speech is sweet and true. 301.
O Victor, you are peerless in form, and with your radiance you illuminate hundreds of fields; O Blessed One, protector of the world like Brahmā and Indra, they all grow dim before your splendor. 302.

O Blessed One with shanks like those of the eneya antelope, you whose gait is like that of the king of elephants, the peacock, and the king of beasts, you look ahead while walking a yoke’s length, making the earth and the slopes of the mountains tremble. 303.
O Blessed One, your body is adorned with the marks; your skin is smooth and golden-hued.
O you who possess a peerless form, the world never reaches satiety in beholding this beauty of yours. (304)

You have practiced austerities for hundreds of previous eons; you delight in total renunciation and the gift of self-control; your mind is filled with compassion and loving-kindness for all sentient beings—I pay homage to you, O Supreme Compassionate One. 305.

You are constantly devoted to generosity and ethical discipline; you are firmly devoted to patience and vigor. You possess the splendor and majesty of meditative concentration and wisdom; I pay homage to you, the bearer of peerless knowledge. 306.
O hero among speakers, crusher of evil factions, you roar like a lion in the assembly;
O King of Physicians, destroyer of the three impurities, I pay homage to you, the bringer of supreme joy. (307)
O Sage, pure in speech, body, and mind, unstained by the three realms of existence like a lotus in the water;
you possess the voice of Brahmā and the song of the kalaviṅka bird—I pay homage to you who have gone beyond the three realms of existence. (308)

You have understood that this world is like an illusion, resembling a theatrical stage or a dream; there is no self, no sentient being, and no life-principle, for all phenomena are like a mirage or the moon reflected in water. 309.

The world wanders in delusion because it does not understand that all things are empty, peaceful, and of the nature of non-arising; yet out of compassion, [the Buddha] leads them into this understanding through hundreds of skillful means, methods, and reasonings. // 310 //

Beholding the world constantly tormented by hundreds of manifold diseases such as passion and the like, you, the peerless and supreme physician, wander through it; O Sugata, liberate hundreds of sentient beings! 311.

O Sage, beholding the world struck by birth, old age, death, and sorrow, and constantly afflicted by hundreds of lamentations and separations from the beloved, you wander about out of compassion, setting it free.
The entire world revolves like a chariot wheel among animals, hungry ghosts, hell-beings, and those in happy migrations;
to those who are deluded, directionless, and without a protector, you reveal the path. (313)
Those former Victors who appeared in the world as lords of Dharma and benefactors of beings—they too proclaimed this very same noble path, which you, O peerless Lord, now likewise teach. (314)

For you utter that speech which is smooth, captivating, excellent, superior even to Brahmā, and supremely pleasing; it utterly surpasses the voices of the Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and the finest Apsarases. 315.

O Victor, having heard your speech— which is purified by truth, uprightness, self-control, and skillful means, and which possesses infinite qualities— hundreds of millions of beings attain peace through the three vehicles.

Through worship of you, they obtain various kinds of divine happiness among human beings; likewise, one becomes a king who brings benefit to the world, wealthy, possessing great riches and vast power. (317)

Even a wheel-turning monarch, a lord of the continents, covers the world with the ten wholesome deeds and obtains the seven most auspicious jewels; but you, O peerless one, generate serene faith in those who behold you. (318)
Through worship of you, one becomes Brahmā, Śakra, the Lord of the World, the Lord of the Saṃtuṣita gods, the Lord of the Paranirmita gods, the Lord of the Suyāma gods, and even a Jina. (319)
Thus, indeed, your worship is unfailing; even the sight of you and the hearing of you are peerless.
You become the remover of the various sufferings of the world, and one who touches the supreme, excellent, and ageless state. 320.
O Knower of the Path, O Skillful in the Path, Blessed One, you turn this world away from evil paths;
O Blessed One, you establish the entire world upon the noble path that is secure, auspicious, and stainless. (321)
For you, a treasury of merit who possesses abundant virtue, the performance of meritorious deeds becomes eternally inexhaustible;
it does not reach exhaustion for many millions of eons until one touches the conduct of enlightenment.
One obtains a beautiful, perfectly pure field that always brings joy, radiant like the Paranirmita heavens;
moreover, in that excellent field, sentient beings become pure in body, speech, and mind. (323)
Thus, a person who performs worship of the Jina obtains manifold virtues such as these;
he attains heaven, liberation, and happiness among humans, becoming a treasury of merit for the entire world. (324)
Your fame and renown have spread extensively throughout hundreds of vast realms in all directions;
the Sugatas, the Jinas, constantly proclaim the garland of your praises within their assemblies. (325)

Free from fever in the world, the bringer of liberation, lovely to behold, supremely compassionate, with senses stilled and delighting in tranquility—O Blessed One, best among the foremost of men, I pay homage to you. 326.

O Victor, having attained the five superknowledges while standing in the sky and having heard your voice, I shall become equal to the Sugatas, O Hero, and I shall distribute the stainless Dharma to the world. (327)

Having today praised the Sugata, who has reached the further shore of all virtues and is honored by humans, gods, and nāgas—may the world attain the vast merit thus acquired, as well as the state of Buddhahood. (328)
Then, Rāṣṭrapāla, at the end of that night, King Arciṣmān heard the sound of weeping in the prince’s inner apartments.
Having heard it, he went quickly and in great haste toward the city of Ratipradhāna. Upon arriving, he said this: "Why, ladies, do you weep?"
They said, "Prince Puṇyaraśmi is not to be seen.
Then, Rāṣṭrapāla, King Arciṣmān fell to the surface of the earth like a tree with its roots severed for the sake of his son.
Rising from the ground, he wandered through that city a thousand times, weeping.
Then, Rāṣṭrapāla, the city deity of that city said this to King Arciṣmān:
"Great King, the prince has gone toward the eastern direction to see, pay homage to, and attend upon the Tathāgata Siddhārthabuddhi."
Then, Rāṣṭrapāla, King Arciṣmān, together with the ladies of his harem and eighty-four hundred thousand nayutas of koṭis of living beings, went toward the eastern direction;
he approached the Tathāgata Siddhārthabuddhi, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of that Blessed One and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, King Arciṣmān praised the Blessed One with these verses:
"I pay homage to the Hero among men, an ocean of virtue and wisdom, for whom there is no equal in this triple world, much less a superior.
Honored by the lords of gods and the kings of asuras, that Supreme Being—no one ever reaches satiety while gazing upon your form. (329)

Your thirty-two bodily marks are perfectly pure, as immaculate as Mount Meru adorned with the finest jewels; smooth, resembling the color of excellent gold, and lovely to the Victors—I pay homage to the body of the Sage, whose appearance is so dear to behold. (330)
For hundreds of inconceivable millions of eons you have observed vows, and for many eons you have honored hundreds of millions of Buddhas;
you have performed hundreds of sacrifices, inconceivable and immeasurable—therefore your body shines forth, beautiful to behold. (331)
Your form is purified by generosity, ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, patience, vigor, meditative absorption, and skillful means;
the radiance of the sun, moon, and jewels does not outshine it, nor does the splendor of Śakra or Brahmā shine before you.
He displays a beautiful form for the sake of the world, resembling a reflection or the moon in water, like an illusion;
yet the body of the Victor is seen in all directions, and yet no measure of form is seen in the Sugatas.
In some places you are seen dwelling among the Tuṣita gods, and again, having assumed the form of a magnificent, pure white elephant;
and yet the hero is seen entering the womb of his mother. O Great Sage, you are omnipresent, like the sky.
In some places you manifest birth; in others, as you travel through the directions, you are seen taking seven steps upon the earth.
Uttering these words—"I am the eldest in the world of men and gods; the supreme deity; I shall liberate the world from the ocean of suffering"—you release your voice. (335)

O Sage, you have no doubt whatsoever regarding the Dharma; yet in the world, you are seen even in the knowledge of scripts and instruction. At times, you are seen having attained the peaceful domain of meditative concentration and absorption, and at other times, you are seen in the midst of women. // 336 //

Having abandoned your mother and father, women, and kinsmen on the earth— stricken with grief, fainting, and wailing— you, the Supreme Being, surrounded by hundreds of millions of gods, are seen departing for the forest dwelling, taking even a single step.
All four Māras have been conquered by you, and for a long time you are seen subduing the Māras within this field.
You turn the inconceivable wheel, yet out of compassion you are seen turning the wheel as it was turned by those of old.

Beholding the world as characterized by the view of eternalism and permanence, you utter the word "nirvāṇa" in the assemblies; yet, constantly beholding the world as delighting in cyclic existence, you speak of the peaceful, cool state of liberation. // 339 //
O Sage, you do not manifest through the mere accumulation of merit, knowledge, skillful means, or wisdom; rather, you radiate from the light of your body throughout many fields.
The Leaders in all directions proclaim your praises; I pay homage to you, the King of Sages, whose range of activity is boundless.
We pay homage to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), which has attained all things; you appear in the activities of all sentient beings like an illusion.
You have no coming from anywhere nor any going anywhere; you abide in the illusory nature of phenomena—to you I bow. 341.
"Excellent, O hero among men, you speak the excellent path by which supreme enlightenment is indeed attained for the sake of the world!
Having quickly awakened to this very nature of phenomena (dharmatā), I too shall teach it, O hero among men, as the nature of phenomena for the sake of the world. (342)

Having praised the All-Knowing One, free from fever, the Hero among men, to whom there is no equal in this triple world, let alone a superior—by whatever merit I have acquired here, may the world touch the peaceful, supreme, and unsurpassed awakening. (343)
Then, Rāṣṭrapāla, the Tathāgata Siddhārthabuddhi, having understood the high resolve of King Arciṣmat, taught the Dharma in such a way that all became irreversible from unexcelled,
perfect enlightenment.
Then, Rāṣṭrapāla, the prince Puṇyaraśmi said this to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Siddhārthabuddhi: "May the Blessed One consent to accept our invitation for a meal tomorrow in our city.
And the Blessed One, out of compassion, consented to Prince Puṇyaraśmi’s request by remaining silent.
Then the prince Puṇyaraśmi addressed his parents and those women: "May you all, together and in harmony, give your approval.
I offer this city, adorned and preeminent in pleasure, to the Tathāgata without regard for it. They gave their approval with one voice.
Then, Rāṣṭrapāla, Prince Puṇyaraśmi, being free from attachment, offered the city of Ratipradhāna, adorned as it was, to the Tathāgata;
and he served that Tathāgata, together with the community of monks, with food arrayed with five hundred flavors.

For all those monks, he had monasteries constructed, piled high with the seven precious gems, provided with jeweled walkways, covered above with canopies of jewel-nets, and beautifully arranged on the left and right with flowering trees.
There were couches and seats adorned with lotus ponds and furnished with hundreds of thousands of spotless cloths spread out on both sides;
and for each individual monk, after he had paid homage, a robe was given to each one.
Every day, robes were offered to one another;
for thirty million years, he did not succumb to sloth and torpor,
nor did he harbor self-love.
He had no other mental engagement regarding the worship of the Buddha;
during this interval, he did not entertain thoughts of sensual desire, nor thoughts of ill will, nor thoughts of cruelty, nor thirst for sovereignty.
He became entirely indifferent toward his body and life, let alone toward any other external thing;
meanwhile, he retained everything that was spoken by the Blessed One.
And that Tathāgata was not questioned a second time; during this interval, he did not bathe, nor did he anoint his limbs with ghee or oil, nor did he wash his feet.
He did not give rise to the perception of fatigue,
nor did he ever sit down, except for the purpose of consuming food and for the purpose of voiding excrement and urine.
And at the time when that Tathāgata passed into parinirvāṇa, at that very time a funeral pyre was prepared from red sandalwood.
On that very spot of earth where that Tathāgata had been cremated, he performed worship of the relics for a hundred thousand years.

Having made every kind of offering and honor to all of Jambūdvīpa with all flowers, all garlands, all perfumes, all musical instruments, and so forth, he subsequently established ninety-four million stūpas.
Those stūpas were composed of the seven precious gems, covered with nets of jewels, and spread over with canopies of pearl nets.
Upon each of the seven-jeweled stūpas, he hoisted five hundred parasols;
at every stūpa, he caused hundreds of thousands of musical instruments to resound;
and throughout Jambudvīpa, he planted trees laden with flowers.

At each [shrine], he burned oil of all fragrances and performed worship with all kinds of perfumes, garlands, and ointments. Having performed worship in this manner for ten million years, he then went forth into the religious life.
Having gone forth, he became one who possessed only the three robes;
he was constantly a beggar for alms and remained in a sitting posture,
never once reclining on his side.
He did not succumb to sloth or torpor.
With that mind free from worldly desire, he gave the gift of Dharma for forty million years,
and yet even at the end, he never [felt weary].
He did not even expect a cry of "well done" from another, much less gain or honor;
nor was he weary from hearing the Dharma or teaching the Dharma.
The deities performed service for him;
and having trained under him, the entire populace, the women of the inner court, all those at his feet, and all his companions went forth as renunciants.

Then, Rāṣṭrapāla, it occurred to the sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host: "The benefactor of the entire kingdom has gone forth into homelessness, training himself in the footsteps of Puṇyaraśmi.
We must perform service and attendance upon him;
thus, service and attendance upon the Three Jewels will have been performed."
Furthermore, after that Tathāgata had passed into parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma remained for sixty-four billion years;
and by the monk Puṇyaraśmi, such worship as this was performed for a thousand Buddhas.
Furthermore, Rāṣṭrapāla, you might perhaps now have some doubt, uncertainty, or hesitation, thinking that the king named Arciṣmān at that time and on that occasion was someone else.
But you should certainly not view it in this way.
Why is that?
At that time, at that very moment, the Tathāgata Amitāyus was a king named Arciṣmān.
Now, Rāṣṭrapāla, you might think that the prince named Puṇyaraśmi at that time, at that moment, was someone else;
however, you must certainly not view it in this way.
For what reason?
Because at that time, on that occasion, I was the prince named Puṇyaraśmi;
and she who was the city goddess—
...became the Tathāgata Akṣobhya.

Therefore, Rāṣṭrapāla, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment should train in the manner of that prince Puṇyaraśmi through the practice of the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) and by relinquishing both the pleasant and the unpleasant.
"By means of heedful conduct [I have realized this]: 'Thus has my unexcelled, perfect enlightenment been attained through the formation of suffering.

Yet those who are not devoted to it—those who value gain, honor, and fame; who are attached to their kinsmen; who are struck down by pride and struck down by gain—these poor souls are ruined; for the sake of gain, they distance themselves from the teaching."

They have renounced the world in vain; they are defilers of the *śramaṇas*, thorns among bodhisattvas, crooked in body, speech, and mind. They are seekers of omens, false in their vows, and fallen from their own commitments. They are obsessed with the signs of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. Shameless and without modesty, lacking virtuous conduct, they are intent upon the false dharma. Devoid of the proper sphere of activity, they have strayed far from the sphere of the Buddhas; they lack the wisdom of the Buddhas, lack the mind of liberation, and lack the mind of awakening.
Therefore, Rāṣṭrapāla, having heard this kind of Dharma, you should understand this: those who seek gain and are intent upon evil friends must not be served.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:

"Though their hearts are fully occupied with gain and fame—which are immeasurable and move the Ten-Powered One—they abandon enlightenment, which is accumulated from hundreds of virtues, and for the sake of profit they become humble before the families of others. (344)

Crows—wicked, devoid of shame and steadfastness, fallen under the sway of Namuci for the sake of their domain, subject to the afflictions and bent toward the realms of existence—speak thus: "We too are possessed of virtues. (345)
Your body is in the forest, yet your mindfulness is in the city; for the sake of gain, you wander amidst conceptual constructions.
Liberation is as far from you as the earth is from the sky; abandon these [desires] like a snake sheds its skin.
The Buddha, the Dharma, and likewise the Saṅgha filled with hundreds of virtues—
having abandoned these, they have departed upon evil paths and are tormented by the eight kinds of afflictions throughout hundreds of existences.
Having heard this account of my conduct as it has been taught, apply yourselves here with a resolute intention through actual practice;

for that which is difficult to attain even in many millions of eons has now been attained in a single moment. Therefore, one should apply oneself here to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) exactly as it has been described. // 348 //
O Lord of the Earth, whoever wishes to awaken to supreme enlightenment in the Supreme Vehicle must be reminded of his qualities:
he should dwell in thorough reflection upon reality as it is; in this way, the unattached enlightenment of the Sugatas is accomplished. (349)
One who perceives virtues should cultivate the noble lineage, generating knowledge therein as if desiring it;
do not thus abandon the teaching, which is the essence of virtue, like fools in all five states of existence. 350.

"Those who dwell here in mountains, forests, and caves, and those who remain there, do not think of me as their self; rather, reproach yourselves, constantly and always recollecting the millions of Buddhas of the past whom you have failed to please. (351)
Abandoning thirst for the body and life, and being without regard for them, one should apply oneself to the Dharma, generating intense reverence;
and the practice has also been taught by me here in this sutra—by abiding in this, awakening will not be difficult for you to attain hereafter. 352.
Those who are disciplined here and rejoiced in the vehicle of the Jina will become very dejected upon hearing [this].
Therefore, one should indeed generate faith in the teaching; do not experience regret later while wandering through existence. (353)
Furthermore, Rāṣṭrapāla, if a bodhisattva were to practice the five perfections,
and another were to accomplish them here through the practice of this Dharma-discourse, thinking, "I shall train in this; I shall abide in this restraint"—

the mass of merit of the former does not approach even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-billionth part of the mass of merit of the latter.

It does not admit of comparison even by number, fraction, calculation, likeness, resemblance, or even a part of a hair’s breadth. Furthermore, while this Dharma discourse was being spoken, thirty million beings— including gods, humans, and asuras— attained the state of non-retrogression regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, a state they had never before attained.
And the minds of seven thousand bhikṣus were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging.
Then the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what is the name of this Dharma-discourse, and how should I remember it?
When this was said, the Blessed One said this to the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla: "Remember it by the name 'The Purification of the Unfailing Vow'."
Remember it as "The Play of the True Being: A Determination of the Bodhisattva’s Conduct," and remember it also as "The Fulfillment of the Purpose."
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla was uplifted, and the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
Thus ends the King of Jewel Sūtras on Previous Lives of the true person Puṇyaraśmi.
The Mahāyāna sūtra entitled "The Inquiry of the Noble Rāṣṭrapāla" is completed.
